2.4.title: Competitive market equilibrium: demand and supply

2.5.title: The role of the price mechanism and market efficiency

2.6.title: Critique of the maximising behaviour of consumers and producers (HL)

T2.1.1.desc: Define a market; local, national and international markets; product and resource markets

T2.1.2.desc: Outline the meaning of a competitive market (competition vs market power)

T2.2.1.desc: Explain the law of demand (individual demand, ceteris paribus, demand schedule)

T2.2.3.desc: Explain the relationship between individual demand and market demand

T2.2.4.desc: Analyse the non-price determinants of demand as causes of demand curve shifts

T2.2.5.desc: Using diagrams, distinguish between movements along and shifts of the demand curve

T2.2.6.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of demand: the law of diminishing marginal utility

T2.2.7.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of demand: the income and substitution effects

T2.3.1.desc: Explain the law of supply (individual supply, supply schedule)

T2.3.2.desc: Draw a supply curve (including the vertical supply curve)

T2.3.3.desc: Explain the relationship between individual supply and market supply

T2.3.4.desc: Analyse the non-price determinants of supply as causes of supply curve shifts

T2.3.5.desc: Using diagrams, distinguish between movements along and shifts of the supply curve

T2.3.6.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of supply: the law of diminishing marginal returns

T2.3.7.desc: (HL) Assumptions underlying the law of supply: increasing marginal costs and the firm's supply curve

T2.4.1.desc: Draw a diagram to illustrate how demand and supply interact to determine market equilibrium

T2.4.2.desc: Analyse demand and supply curve shifts that give rise to a new equilibrium, using excess demand (shortage) and excess supply (surplus)

T2.4.3.desc: Draw diagrams to illustrate how shifts in demand and supply give rise to a new equilibrium (incl. free and economic goods)

T2.5.1.desc: Analyse the price mechanism: resource allocation through the signalling and incentive functions of prices

T2.5.2.desc: Analyse the price mechanism: rationing (price and non-price rationing)

T2.5.3.desc: Explain consumer surplus, producer surplus and social (community) surplus (MB and MC interpretation of demand and supply)

T2.5.4.desc: Draw a diagram showing maximum social surplus at competitive market equilibrium

T2.5.5.desc: Explain the conditions for allocative efficiency at competitive market equilibrium (MB = MC, maximum social surplus) and why intervention may still be needed

T2.6.1.desc: Evaluate the assumptions of consumer rationality, utility maximisation and perfect information

T2.6.2.desc: Behavioural critique: biases (rules of thumb, anchoring, framing, availability)

T2.6.3.desc: Behavioural critique: bounded rationality, bounded self-control, bounded selfishness, imperfect information

T2.6.4.desc: Policies inspired by behavioural economics: nudge theory

T2.6.5.desc: Policies inspired by behavioural economics: choice architecture (default, restricted and mandated choice)

T2.6.6.desc: Evaluate behavioural economics and its policies (mainstream response, advantages, disadvantages)

T2.6.8.desc: Alternative business objectives: corporate social responsibility, market share, growth, satisficing (and revenue maximisation)

T3.1.1.desc: Define PED and identify the various degrees and range of values for PED (sign, use of percentages)

T3.1.2.desc: Draw diagrams showing the range of values for PED (relatively elastic and inelastic; perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, unitary) and PED versus steepness

T3.1.3.desc: (HL) Explain and illustrate changing PED along a straight-line downward-sloping demand curve

T3.1.5.desc: Explain the relationship between PED and total revenue

T3.1.6.desc: Draw a diagram to show how total revenue changes in response to a price change with elastic, inelastic or unit elastic demand

T3.1.7.desc: Apply PED: its importance for firms (pricing) and government decision-making (indirect taxes)

T3.1.8.desc: (HL) Analyse why primary commodities generally have a lower PED than manufactured products (and the consequences for prices and producer revenues)

T3.2.1.desc: Define YED and, depending on the sign of YED, distinguish between normal and inferior goods

T3.2.2.desc: Depending on the value of YED (less than or greater than one), distinguish between necessities, luxuries and services

T3.2.3.desc: Draw an Engel curve diagram to show income elastic, income inelastic and inferior goods

T3.2.4.desc: (HL) Apply YED: discuss its relevance to firms

T3.2.5.desc: (HL) Apply YED: discuss changes in the sectoral structure of an economy

T3.3.1.desc: Define PES and identify the various degrees and range of values for PES

T3.3.2.desc: Draw diagrams showing the range of values for PES (relatively elastic and inelastic; perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, unitary)

T3.3.4.desc: (HL) Apply PES: why primary commodities generally have a lower PES than manufactured products (and the consequences)
